set.prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(c)(1): private residential projects built on private property are not subject to prevailing wage unless built under an agreement with a state agency, a redevelopment agency or successor agency, or a local public housing authority (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). The ADU Guidelines V2 adopted by the Board on March 10, 2026 (Legistar matter 26-308, https://napa.legistar1.com/napa/attachments/201f9d80-fbde-4df8-9dd9-b7548f13765b.pdf) attach the loan documents, and the only public party is the County of Napa: the Accessory Dwelling Unit Loan Agreement (Exhibit B, p. 14) is between the County of Napa, a political subdivision, and the Borrower, and is signed for the County by the County Executive Officer with County Counsel approval (p. 24); the Deed of Trust names the County of Napa as beneficiary, and the Regulatory Agreement and Promissory Note run to the County. The Napa County Housing Authority is not a party. The borrower must own and occupy the single-family home on whose lot the ADU is built (Loan Agreement Recital C), so 1720(c)(1) applies and the forgivable loan, though public funds under 1720(b), does not trigger prevailing wage. 1720(c)(5)(C) (assistance for rehabilitation of a single-family home) is not relied on because the program funds new ADU construction. The program documents contain no prevailing wage provision. A project that also used state agency or Housing Authority funds would need a new review.
set.audit_note: Prevailing wage re-checked November 10, 2026 against the loan documents attached to the V2 guidelines (matter 26-308): loan agreement, deed of trust, regulatory agreement and note are all with the County of Napa, not the Housing Authority, so the trigger stays false under Labor Code 1720(c)(1). Award terms verified against the same guidelines.

reason: Loan agreement template names and is signed by the County of Napa, not the Housing Authority, so 1720(c)(1) applies; basis rewritten with document citations and stale audit_note fixed.

set.typical_award_size: Services: up to $250,000 per year for homeless prevention and rapid rehousing (FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 CDC NOFAs). Development: LMIHAF housing development spending was $3,837,187 in FY 2024-25 and $1,316,702 in FY 2023-24; the annual reports do not break this out by project or award size. Balance available for all other uses $2,509,338 at June 30, 2025 (down from $7,248,573 at June 30, 2024), of which $1,509,338 is excess surplus; loans and grants receivable $31,242,980.
set.affordability_requirement: Community Redevelopment Law housing provisions as applied by HSC 34176.1 (very low and low income). For development spending, at least 30 percent must go to rental housing for households at or below 30% AMI (FY 2024-25 report, Note 9); the report states Casa Roseland, under construction, has 32 percent of units at or below 30% AMI. Current NOFA awards are homeless services.
set.layering_notes: The Sonoma County Community Development Commission, parent entity of the Sonoma County Housing Authority, is the housing successor. The fund pays for services through the annual CDC NOFA and also finances development directly: $3,837,187 of housing development spending in FY 2024-25 and $1,316,702 in FY 2023-24. The FY 2024-25 report lists Roseland Village (665 Sebastopol Road, Santa Rosa, a former RDA property) and Casa Roseland as under construction but does not tie the development spending to a named project. Its plan for the $1,509,338 excess surplus (held more than 6 years) is reinvestment in affordable homeownership loans and/or new construction or preservation of affordable rental developments, so capital money is possible but is not offered through a posted competitive round. Former RDA Reinvestment and Revitalization money flows into CFH instead. Loan repayments ($31.2M receivable) replenish the fund. The FY 2025-26 report was not posted as of November 10, 2026.
set.prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). The FY 2024-25 Housing Successor Agency Annual Report (https://sonomacounty.gov/Main%20County%20Site/Development%20Services/CDC/Documents/Successor%20Agency/Housing%20Successor%20Agency%20Annual%20Reports/Remediated_FY%2024-25%20Housing%20Successor%20Agency%20Annual%20Report.pdf) states no prevailing wage rule. Homelessness prevention and rapid rehousing grants are not construction under 1720(a)(1), but the fund paid $3,837,187 for housing development in FY 2024-25. The 1720(c)(1) private residential exemption does not apply to projects built under an agreement with a successor agency to a redevelopment agency or a local public housing authority, and the housing successor here is the Community Development Commission, parent entity of the Sonoma County Housing Authority, so a development agreement with it should not be assumed exempt under 1720(c)(1). 1720(c)(4) names only the former redevelopment Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund, not housing successor asset funds. Below-market loans can be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) (at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI), as DIR PW 2019-018 applied (https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf). Land transfers below fair market value are public funds under 1720(b)(3).
set.audit_note: Corrected November 10, 2026: the FY 2024-25 and FY 2023-24 Housing Successor annual reports show LMIHAF development spending ($3,837,187 and $1,316,702), so the record no longer says the fund is not used for development. FY 2025-26 report not yet posted. Prevailing wage left unclear: no LMIHAF document states a rule, 1720(c)(1) likely unavailable because the housing successor is the CDC (parent of the Housing Authority), and 1720(c)(5)(E) turns on project facts.
